cards.title: Introduction to Caching
cards.content: Caching stores copies of frequently accessed data in a fast-access storage layer (like memory) to reduce database load and speed up response times in your Flask application.

options.text: To permanently store user passwords in plain text
To speed up data retrieval by storing temporary copies of data
To compile Python code into machine language
To route incoming HTTP requests to different controllers

cards.title: Setting Up Flask-Caching
cards.content:
To use caching in Flask, we typically use the Flask-Caching extension.

from flask import Flask
from flask_caching import Cache

app = Flask(__name__)
cache = Cache(app, config={'CACHE_TYPE': 'SimpleCache'})

cards.title: Complete the Cache Initialization
cards.content: To initialize the cache extension, we instantiate the {blank} class passing the app object.

cards.title: Caching View Functions
cards.content:
You can cache the output of route handlers using the @cache.cached() decorator.

@app.route('/')
@cache.cached(timeout=50)
def index():
    return expensive_database_query()

steps: Client sends an HTTP request to a Flask route
Flask checks if the response exists in the cache
If cached, return the stored response immediately
If not cached, execute the view function, store result in cache, and return response

cards.title: Memoization with cache.memoize
cards.content:
Use @cache.memoize() when you want to cache the results of functions that take arguments, such as database queries filtered by an ID.

@cache.memoize(timeout=60)
def get_user_profile(user_id):
    return User.query.get(user_id)

cards.title: Caching Best Practices
cards.content:
1. Don't cache user-specific sensitive data globally.
2. Always set an appropriate timeout.
3. Implement cache invalidation strategies when underlying data updates.
